title: Stupni Do: The Massacre Near Vares
content:
On 23 October 1993, HVO forces attacked the Bosniak village of Stupni Do, situated in a narrow valley near the central Bosnian town of Vares. The assault, carried out by special purpose units operating under the command of HVO colonel Ivica Rajic, resulted in the killing of at least thirty-seven people, including approximately thirty-one civilians, and the near-total destruction of the village. The ICTY Rajic Sentencing Judgment (IT-95-12-S) documented the attack following Rajic's guilty plea to persecution as a crime against humanity.

Stupni Do was a small Bosniak settlement of perhaps fifty houses, home to several hundred people. The village's vulnerability was a product of the broader fragmentation of central Bosnia in 1993, where Bosniak and Croat communities found themselves on opposite sides of a conflict that had erupted within territories they had previously shared. Vares itself was an unusual municipality -- an industrial town with a significant Croat population that had initially resisted the HVO's confrontation with the ARBiH. By October 1993, however, hardline HVO commanders had asserted control, and the moderate local leadership that had sought coexistence was sidelined.

The attack on Stupni Do was carried out by the "Maturice" special purpose unit, a formation with a reputation for brutality that had been deployed to the Vares area to enforce HVO authority. The assault began in the morning and continued through the day. Soldiers moved through the village killing civilians, including women, children, and elderly residents. Houses were systematically set ablaze. The destruction was thorough enough that when investigators eventually reached the site, much of the physical evidence had been consumed by fire.

What distinguished the immediate aftermath of Stupni Do from other atrocities in the war was the deliberate obstruction of international investigation. Nordic Battalion (NordBat) soldiers from UNPROFOR, stationed in the Vares area, attempted to reach the village within hours of the attack. HVO forces physically blocked their access, maintaining roadblocks and refusing passage for several days. When UNPROFOR personnel finally entered Stupni Do, they documented scenes consistent with a systematic attack on a civilian population -- burned structures, human remains, and evidence of execution-style killings.

In nearby Vares itself, over 250 Bosniak men were rounded up and subjected to what the ICTY record described as inhuman treatment, including beatings and detention in degrading conditions. The roundup reflected a broader pattern of collective punishment directed against the Bosniak civilian population of the municipality.

The consequences of the Stupni Do massacre extended beyond the immediate victims. The attack and its aftermath effectively sealed the fate of the Croat community in Vares. When ARBiH forces advanced on the town in early November 1993, the bulk of the Croat population fled, fearing retribution. Vares, which had been one of the few municipalities in central Bosnia where some semblance of inter-ethnic coexistence had persisted into mid-1993, was emptied of its Croat residents in a matter of days. The HVO's own atrocity had precipitated the displacement of the community it claimed to protect.

Ivica Rajic was initially indicted by the ICTY but evaded arrest for years, living under a false identity. He eventually surrendered and pleaded guilty to one count of persecution as a crime against humanity, receiving a twelve-year sentence. His guilty plea spared a full trial but confirmed the essential facts: that the attack on Stupni Do was a deliberate assault on a civilian population, ordered by the local HVO command, and executed with calculated brutality.
